episode_title: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset

stories.summary: As a schoolboy in the 'Hum Do Hamare Do' era of family planning, Amit was taught that India was poor because it had too many people. It felt intuitive: a poor country, not enough to go around. Only as he came into adulthood did he realise the opposite was true. He grew angrier as he saw most people still holding the belief and refusing to adjust their views to the facts.
stories.insight: Ideas absorbed in childhood feel like common sense because nobody ever asks us to check them. The intuitive story of a fixed pie and too many mouths can be the exact reverse of what the evidence shows.
stories.quote: When we were in school we were told India's great problem is population. Why are we poor? There are too many people, right? And that is a canard that we were fed

stories.topic: Paul Ehrlich's Taxi Ride Through Delhi
stories.summary: Amit reads the passage from The Population Bomb in which Paul Ehrlich says he had long understood the population explosion 'intellectually' but only came to understand it 'emotionally' in an ancient taxi crawling through a crowded Delhi slum: fleas on the seats, over a hundred degrees, dust and smoke, and 'people, people, people, people.' Ehrlich wondered whether they would ever reach the hotel. He also wrote that he couldn't see how India could feed 200 million more people by 1980. Amit notes that Delhi's population has since grown about five times, and argues Ehrlich was embellishing because mid-60s Delhi wasn't that crowded.
stories.insight: The most influential population panic of its era rested on a visceral recoil from crowds of poor people, not on evidence. The city that horrified Ehrlich went on to absorb many times more people.
stories.quote: the population of Delhi has in that time exploded five times from what it was when Ehrlich had his taxi ride, about which he is clearly lying, because in the mid sixties Delhi wasn't that overpopulated.

stories.summary: Reading from Coomi Kapoor's The Emergency, Amit describes how Sanjay Gandhi, acting as an extra-constitutional authority, pushed family planning, which also earned international credibility because bodies like the Ford Foundation were pressing for it. He bypassed the nodal ministry and went straight to chief ministers eager to please him, Bansi Lal of Haryana most notoriously. Sterilisations rose from 26.24 lakh in 1975-76 to 81.32 lakh in 1976-77, and Haryana hit four times its target. Every district and officer had quotas, and missing them meant withheld salaries, suspensions and transfers. The pressure flowed down to police and junior staff. Teachers had to 'motivate' at least five sterilisations to get paid, and some offered half their salaries to find volunteers. A third or fourth child could be refused admission to government school without a sterilisation certificate. Loans, land and jobs were tied to certificates, and some Delhi government hospitals refused treatment until the patient agreed to be sterilised. Police opened fire at least eight times between August and December 1976.
stories.insight: Once a policy becomes a numerical target passed down a hierarchy, every link in the chain has a reason to coerce the next one. The cruelty comes from how the incentives are designed, not from a few bad apples.
stories.quote: Some desperate teachers were so frantic to meet their quotas that they offered half their salaries to persuade volunteers to undergo the operation.

stories.summary: In Pipli, a Haryana village 45 km north of Delhi, a widower named Hawa Singh was forcibly taken for sterilisation. His incision turned septic and he bled to death. The block development officer still came back for more 'volunteers' and picked up a man repairing shoes by the roadside. Villagers drove the officials out. Several hundred policemen then besieged the village overnight. At 6 am they opened fire, killing two women making cow-dung cakes outside their huts, and threatened to send an aircraft to bomb the area. Out of a population of 2,761, between 400 and 500 men were rounded up and sterilised. Amit adds that sterilisation incentives continue across rural India today, and that it is always women who suffer most.
stories.insight: Even if you believe population is a problem, coercive family planning tells citizens that the state, not they, owns their bodies. Amit calls this worse than slavery, and notes how normalised it became.
stories.quote: The intrinsic message being sent out by the state is that you do not own your bodies.

stories.summary: Paul Ehrlich once declared that if he were a gambler, he'd take even money that England would not exist in the year 2000. Economist Julian Simon noticed the word 'bet' and publicly challenged him. Ehrlich could choose five resources and any period longer than a year. Simon would bet (around $10,000, as Amit recalls) that their prices would fall instead of rising with scarcity. Ehrlich picked copper, chromium, nickel, tin and tungsten. The bet was made in 1980, and by 1990 all five were cheaper. Ehrlich nonetheless remains a major figure and, Amit says, 'a hero of the left even today.'
stories.insight: Betting on a prediction exposes doom narratives to reality. Scarcity sets off human ingenuity and price adjustment, so resources don't simply run out as people multiply. Being spectacularly wrong rarely costs a public intellectual his standing.
stories.quote: Paul Ehrlich at one point remarks, if I were a gambler, I would take even money that England will not exist in the year two thousand.

stories.topic: A PhD on Fertility, and Poland's Birth Strike
stories.summary: Offering what he calls 'an amusing fact', Ajay reveals that his PhD thesis was on fertility, specifically women in Malaysia having babies, which took him deep into the fertility literature. His favourite story from it is about Poland. A young country carved out by the Treaty of Versailles, it was immediately invaded by the Soviets, with Leon Trotsky stopped at its edges. It then lived precariously between Germany and the Soviet Union, neither of which could be trusted as a neighbour. Under that constant sense that something would go wrong, birth rates collapsed, and this happened without any modern reproductive technology.
stories.insight: Fertility tracks how people see the future. Dread alone can make a society stop having children, with no pill required.
stories.quote: When hope dies, you stop having children. Okay. So having children is an act of hope.

stories.topic: The Idle Young Men of Bihar
stories.summary: Amit's friend Kumar Anand described travelling through semi-urban Bihar near Saharsa, where he lives, and seeing streets full of young men standing around. They weren't waiting for a bus, smoking at a katta, or waiting for a contractor's truck to take them to work. They were just standing, idle. Kumar Anand and Mohit Satyanand later did a road-trip episode on Bihar for The Seen and the Unseen, and much of what they described was young people who either have no jobs or no longer care.
stories.insight: A demographic dividend without jobs turns into a demographic disaster. Hopeless young men don't dream of building families, which feeds the very fertility and social problems Ajay warns about.
stories.quote: They're just standing. They're just idle and you know, and it was a haunting image the way he described it.

stories.topic: Julian Simon's 'I Told You So' to Milton Friedman
stories.summary: In December 1976, a young Julian Simon wrote to Milton Friedman about his plan for airline overbooking. When a flight is oversold, passengers write sealed bids of the lowest amount they'd accept to take the next flight, and the low bidders are paid and rebooked. He asked Friedman to vouch to the Civil Aeronautics Board that it wasn't the work of a crank. Friedman replied that the plan made sense to every economist, but he declined to write. He reasoned that if it were that good, airlines would already be doing it, so 'we must be overlooking something.' Then Alfred E. Kahn, an economist, was appointed head of the CAB, and airlines adopted the scheme. In 1979 Simon sent Friedman American Airlines' glowing report on it. Friedman replied with a short, gracious letter.
stories.insight: Two great minds disagreed and then settled it with no ego involved: the senior figure openly conceded and credited the junior one. In a polarised age where people dread being seen to be wrong in public, that grace is rare and worth copying.
stories.quote: Many thanks for your I told you so, you are entitled to it. You deserve a great deal of credit for having pushed your idea as effectively as you have.

recommendations.item: Population Is Not a Problem, but Our Greatest Strength
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Listed as essential reading. Amit says he has written a number of columns on the subject because it is one of his biggest bugbears.
recommendations.reason: The written version of the episode's argument: population density drives prosperity, and the ills blamed on population are really failures of governance.

recommendations.item: The Ultimate Resource
recommendations.creator: Julian Simon
recommendations.context: Amit cites Simon's 1981 book (later released in a second edition) as the best phrasing of what he believes.
recommendations.reason: Its thesis that human beings are the ultimate resource is the root of the 'people are brains, not stomachs' worldview.

recommendations.item: Too Many People?
recommendations.creator: Nicholas Eberstadt
recommendations.context: Amit opens his case with this 2007 study.
recommendations.reason: It finds no correlation between population density and poverty, with striking counterexamples: Monaco is forty times as dense as Bangladesh and far richer, and Bahrain is three times as dense as India and far richer.

recommendations.item: The Great Breakthrough and Its Cause
recommendations.creator: Julian Simon
recommendations.context: Amit mentions Simon's last book, edited and finished by Timur Kuran, Ajay's former professor.
recommendations.reason: It extends Simon's argument that the industrial revolution and productivity booms happened because population rose. More people multiply the opportunities for free trade and voluntary exchange, and everyone benefits.

recommendations.item: An Essay on the Principle of Population
recommendations.creator: Thomas Robert Malthus
recommendations.context: Amit traces modern population pessimism back to this 1798 essay.
recommendations.reason: Read it to see where the idea began: Malthus claimed people grow exponentially while resources grow arithmetically, so mass starvation was inevitable.

recommendations.item: The Population Bomb
recommendations.creator: Paul Ehrlich
recommendations.context: Amit reads its opening lines and Ehrlich's Delhi taxi passage.
recommendations.reason: A case study in confident doom. It declared the battle to feed humanity already lost and predicted hundreds of millions would starve in the 1970s and 80s, which never happened.

recommendations.item: The Book That Incited a Worldwide Fear of Overpopulation
recommendations.creator: Charles Mann
recommendations.context: Amit quotes Mann on the population-control movements of the 1950s–70s, led by bodies like the Rockefeller and Ford Foundations.
recommendations.reason: It shows the global scale of the coercion: health workers paid per IUD inserted, birth-control pills pitched out of helicopters over villages in the Philippines, and millions sterilised, often coercively, from Mexico to Bangladesh.

recommendations.item: The Emergency: A Personal History
recommendations.creator: Coomi Kapoor
recommendations.context: Amit names it as one of his recommendations for the episode and reads at length from its chapter on Sanjay Gandhi and family planning.
recommendations.reason: A great journalist's first-hand account of how the sterilisation drive spun out of control: quotas, withheld salaries, denied medical care, police firings and the siege of Pipli.

recommendations.item: Coomi Kapoor Has the Inside Track (Episode 305 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit notes that Coomi Kapoor has also been a guest on The Seen and the Unseen.
recommendations.reason: A long-form conversation with the author of The Emergency, for anyone who wants more from her.

recommendations.item: The Simon–Ehrlich wager
recommendations.context: A show-notes link for the bet Amit narrates.
recommendations.reason: Background on the 1980 wager in which all five metals Ehrlich chose (copper, chromium, nickel, tin and tungsten) were cheaper by 1990.

recommendations.item: Triumph of the City
recommendations.creator: Edward Glaeser
recommendations.context: Ajay says he built his intuition about density from this book.
recommendations.reason: It explains that cities are great because they pack large numbers of clever people close together. It also admits dense cities can be terrible (crime, slums, public health), which makes good governance the real challenge.

recommendations.item: The Skeptical Environmentalist
recommendations.creator: Bjørn Lomborg
recommendations.context: Amit cites it while discussing how messy cities improve over time.
recommendations.reason: It taught him that cities follow an arc: London around the turn of the 19th century was as polluted and overrun as any Indian city today, and it later became much cleaner.

recommendations.item: The Origins of Totalitarianism
recommendations.creator: Hannah Arendt
recommendations.context: Ajay's book recommendation for the episode. He had earlier drawn on Arendt to argue that totalitarian regimes depopulate.
recommendations.reason: Arendt was among the first to show how much Nazi Germany and Stalin's Russia had in common, which makes her an essential guide to authoritarian regimes. Amit adds that it is not a book of history but 'a book of the present moment.'

recommendations.item: Yuganta
recommendations.creator: Irawati Karve
recommendations.context: Amit's book recommendation for the episode.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a masterpiece that made him understand his society and culture far better. It is literary criticism of our epics and the role of women in them, sometimes disquieting to read. It is also an analysis of a society we still live in, not of another time and place.

recommendations.item: What Bruce Springsteen Means to Us (Episode 13 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay recalls the 'two beautiful sentences' by Bruce Springsteen that Amit had read, about a child being another shot.
recommendations.reason: Springsteen's idea of a child as 'another shot' anchors Ajay's argument that having a child is an act of optimism.

recommendations.item: The State of the Ukraine War (Episode 14 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside Ajay's discussion of the war's demographic toll on Russia.
recommendations.reason: Context for Ajay's estimate that about 300,000 Russian men of reproductive age have died and about a million of Russia's best and brightest have left. That loss will reshape Russia's demographics.

recommendations.item: Understanding Baumol's Cost Disease And Its Impact On Healthcare
recommendations.creator: Varun Ganapathi
recommendations.context: Ajay urges listeners to 'please go study Baumol's cost disease' while explaining the economics of an ageing society. The show notes link this essay.
recommendations.reason: He calls it 'one of those great ideas in economics.' It bears directly on his point that personal services for the elderly, which only young people can provide, become unaffordable when the young are scarce.

recommendations.item: The Evil of Family Planning
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentions his 2014 column, written after several women died because sterilisations were done in unhygienic conditions.
recommendations.reason: His earlier case that sterilisation camps and incentives still operate in India today, long after the Emergency.

recommendations.item: Economic Learnings of India for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Bihar (Episode 345 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The road-trip episode on Bihar with Mohit Satyanand and Kumar Anand that Amit refers to.
recommendations.reason: Much of what the guests describe is young people without jobs who have lost hope. It is the human face of a demographic dividend turning into a disaster.

recommendations.item: The Effect of Age-Specific Sex Ratios on Crime: Instrumental Variable Estimates from India
recommendations.creator: Rashmi Barua, Prarthna Goel and Renuka Sane
recommendations.context: Ajay cites the paper co-authored by 'our friend' Renuka Sane.
recommendations.reason: Using an interesting identification strategy, it finds that when the sex ratio tilts toward excess males, crime rises.

core_ideas.explanation: A person is not just a mouth to feed but a mind that creates. More people mean bigger networks, more positive-sum games and more mutually beneficial trades. Amit also sees a moral problem in population pessimism: calling population a problem means calling other people the problem while placing yourself above it.
core_ideas.quote: More people mean greater networks, more positive sum games, more double thank you moments.

core_ideas.concept: Voting With Your Feet Toward Density
core_ideas.explanation: If density caused poverty, people would flee crowded places. Instead, all of human history is migration from sparse villages to dense cities: people go from Bihar to Mumbai, not the reverse. Even a Mumbai slum beats the village for those who choose it. Amit's challenge to the listener: if you're in a city, why are you there? And if you're in a village, you either made your money in a city or want to go to one.
core_ideas.quote: But the whole story of humanity, all of human history, is about migrating from sparsely populated rural areas to cities with dense populations.

core_ideas.concept: Urban Agglomeration Is the Engine of Modernity
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues a city's greatness is the number of clever people living within 20 minutes of you, and the combined human capital that challenges and drives you. We are each creatures of the people around us. Scatter everyone onto a 100-metre grid and that flowering dies. Modern culture is urban, created in dense collections of people, not in the landowner machismo of rural life.
core_ideas.quote: So it's the number of people that live within 20 minutes of you. Okay, that is the greatness of a city.

core_ideas.explanation: The poverty, slums, crime and pollution we blame on population are really failures of governance. Glaeser shows dense cities can be terrible, and New York in the 70s was famous for crime, rats and cockroaches. Lomborg shows London was once as polluted as any Indian city today. Ajay cautions that improvement is not inevitable and takes purposeful action, but cities around the world have fixed these problems and the know-how exists.
core_ideas.quote: You need to get your public health right. You need to do urban planning for the transportation and the parks, but these are not beyond the wit of man

core_ideas.explanation: Malthusian doom comes from projecting a growth curve into infinity, as with Malthus's claim that people grow exponentially while resources grow arithmetically, or the doomsayers' vision of 70 billion people visiting each other by elevator because there are no roads. Julian Simon mocked this by noting that if the recent growth of university buildings continued, one day the earth would be nothing but university buildings. We think in zero-sum terms, but human ingenuity and the price system respond to scarcity by finding alternatives.
core_ideas.quote: anyone statistically knows that you cannot extrapolate a trend and assume that it will continue forever.

core_ideas.concept: Why the Poor Have More Children
core_ideas.explanation: Poor families treat children as resources, which is itself evidence that people are assets. High child mortality made extra children a form of insurance. Yet even with child mortality far lower today, the poor still have more children and the rich fewer.
core_ideas.quote: why do poor people have more children? Because they are viewing children as resources.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay compares family planning in pre-Emergency India (modest coercion), Emergency India (terrible, subject to the whims of one or two people) and communist China (the one-child policy, draconian beyond belief). The more concentrated the power, the further a mistaken idea escalates into disaster. That is the case for dispersing power and making such state intrusion illegitimate.
core_ideas.quote: many terrible ideas become accepted because nobody has the guts to tell the dictator that you're full of it.

core_ideas.explanation: Coercion comes in degrees of intrusiveness. Stopping a Punjab farmer from burning his field is mild. Telling a single woman she cannot use surrogacy is a different order of evil, because it reaches into personal life. Amit makes the same point about forced sterilisation: the state tells you that you do not own your body. Whether to have children should be the business of individuals alone.
core_ideas.quote: I have no children today, but that's my goddamn birthright.

core_ideas.concept: There Is No Budget Constraint on Coercion
core_ideas.explanation: Government spending has a built-in brake: extracting taxes is hard, and people resist, move money abroad or hide it, so even a half-witted government weighs what it spends. Coercion has no such limit. Governments can pile one coercive rule on another with no cap on the total and little sense of degree. So citizens must push back much harder against intrusive coercion.
core_ideas.quote: There's no budget constraint in coercion.

core_ideas.concept: Having a Child Is an Act of Hope
core_ideas.explanation: Drawing on Hannah Arendt's point that totalitarians run out of people to oppress, Ajay argues that tyranny breeds hopelessness and stagnation, and men and women respond by going on a birth strike. Russia shows it now: about 300,000 men of reproductive age have died in Ukraine and about a million of the best and brightest have left, about 1.3 million people, and with them a future stream of children. Such collapses happened long before modern contraception existed.
core_ideas.quote: Tyranny creates hopelessness. And having a child is an act of hope.

core_ideas.concept: Fear the Population Bust, Not the Boom
core_ideas.explanation: The real danger is a sharp fall in fertility. The US and UK declined slowly, giving society generations to adjust. In China and Russia the children vanished suddenly, leaving few young people and many old ones, which is wrenching for a society.
core_ideas.quote: And far from the fears of a population bomb. Today we understand the damage from a population bust

core_ideas.concept: The Arithmetic of an Ageing Society
core_ideas.explanation: Set pensions and financial wealth aside and look only at people. The elderly need nursing, cooking, cleaning and personal care, which only the young can provide. If 10 old people need the services of 15 young people, that works. When the old share balloons and they need 60 young people's services, it becomes impossible, because the young must also produce everything else. These services can't be imported, so their prices shoot towards infinity and few elderly can afford dignity.
core_ideas.quote: anything produced by the young faces this exchange rate problem, that how many young people are available to produce it? How many old people are there to buy it?

core_ideas.explanation: India's last census was in 2011, with no 2021 census in sight, and its statistics are weak across the board: census data has even been manipulated to draw electoral maps, and GDP, industrial production, NSSO and ASI figures are poorly measured. Even so, alternative sources point to a rapid fall in fertility over the last 10–15 years. Ajay attributes it to how would-be parents read their world: cramped urban housing, long commutes, a skewed sex ratio, the norm of needing a job before marriage amid poor employment, and an ever-interfering state.
core_ideas.quote: Do they see jobs? Do they see freedom? Do they see safety? Or do they see a grim, troubled world where there is social strife, an ever-interfering state, and poor economic prospects?

core_ideas.concept: Loosen the Rules on Who Can Raise Children
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that having more children should be a good thing for those who choose it, that government should never limit that choice, and that society shouldn't insist only a father and mother can raise a child. Opening up to single parents and other unconventional arrangements would reflect the blossoming of human freedom. It would also be practical in a country facing a fertility problem.
core_ideas.quote: we should not tie ourselves around heteronormative family concepts.

core_ideas.concept: Bare Branches: When the Dividend Becomes a Disaster
core_ideas.explanation: The Chinese 'bare branches' problem refers to young men who never find their feet, never learn a trade, earn an income, move out or build a family. Renuka Sane and her co-authors find that more men relative to women means more crime. Amit adds a neuroscience point he recalls (possibly from Robert Sapolsky): the brain region responsible for socialisation in males fully develops only around 25, which is why most violence comes from males aged 18–25. Ajay adds that raising boys without talking to girls is 'a dagger wound on the soul.' Without jobs, Amit concludes, the demographic dividend becomes a demographic disaster.
core_ideas.quote: no amount of government dole is a substitute for standing on your own feet and learning a trade and developing an income.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Noticing that the hosts are wearing matching shirts, Ajay asks: 'What spontaneous banter can we do about this spontaneous order?'

Amit says the design on Ajay's shirt reminds him of 'maggots on a dead cow,' then reveals the source: twentieth-century population pessimist Harrison Brown, who wrote that humanity 'will not rest content until the earth is covered completely and to a considerable depth with a writhing mass of human beings, much as a dead cow is covered with a pulsating mass of maggots.'

After reading Ehrlich's anguished 'Would we ever get to our hotel?', Amit deadpans: 'And I'm pleased to report he did get to his hotel.' Later he adds that Ehrlich is still a hero of the left even though 'he has been wrong about everything in his life.'
Ajay on botched sterilisation camps: 'the autoclave will not be working, the instruments will be contaminated. That's garden variety incompetence of the Indian state. That's unsurprising.'

Ajay on India's statistics: 'The bad news to you, Virginia, if you believed that the Indian census was gospel truth. It's not.' He adds that Indian-style gerrymandering works by manipulating the census rather than by redrawing constituencies.
Amit: 'I sometimes provocatively say that most Urdu poetry is a whining of incels, but you know, that is just a provocation, but the whining of incels could kinda become a problem.'
Amit on gender segregation: 'I went to a boys' school. I learned how to talk to girls by watching Bollywood, which is not quite the best thing, is it?'

Julian Simon's gloat-without-gloating letter to Milton Friedman: 'I'm one of your great fans, and I'm not an I told you so type. Still, you may find it interesting to compare your second and third paragraphs...'

Amit on Alfred E. Kahn, the economist whose appointment to the Civil Aeronautics Board let Simon's overbooking auction happen: 'he's a good economist because not all economists get economics, but he's a good economist. He gets it.'
'Hum Do Hamare Do' ('We two, our two'), the family-planning slogan Amit grew up with and the canard he wants to dismantle.

Malthus's notorious line from his 1798 essay: 'Instead of recommending cleanliness to the poor, we should encourage contrary habits and court the return of the plague,' because for him the plague would be deliverance.
Robert Sapolsky, probably on an episode of Sam Harris's podcast ('I might be misremembering'), is Amit's source for the claim that the socialising part of the male brain matures only around 25.
